notes.title: Chapter map: Performance & profiling

headings.text: 🌳 Where should the performance effort go?

notes.html:
One cost model and the tools to act on it: Python charges per interpreted step, so every note is either measuring where the steps are (59, 60) or having fewer of them (58, 61, 62). Read each arrow as a sentence: profiling built on why Python is slow.

Green = CORE, blue = SUPPORTING, yellow = BREADTH, grey = another chapter (dashed edges).

Reading order: 58 why Python is slow ─▶ 59 profiling ─▶ 60 micro-optimization traps ─▶ 61 the native boundary ─▶ 62 interpreter speedups

🌳 Where should the performance effort go?

The levers in this chapter are alternatives, ordered by payoff, so the tree lives here, not in each note.

What each leaf is, and the one condition that would change the answer:

  • ⏳ concurrency (async or threads): if the waiting is on a dependency that's itself saturated, more concurrency adds queueing, not throughput; fix or cache the dependency.

  • 🔬 profile at real size (profiling): if the slowness only shows in production, sample the live process with py-spy instead of reproducing it locally.

  • 🧮 fix the algorithm (why Python is slow): if n is genuinely small and bounded, the O(n²) may be fine; spend the effort elsewhere.

  • ⚡ vectorize or batch (why Python is slow): if each call handles under ~200 items, the boundary costs more than the work; batch harder first.

  • 🌉 native extension (the native boundary): if the team can't own a build toolchain and wheels, use a process pool or free-threaded build instead.

  • 🏭 process pool (multiprocessing): if pickling inputs costs more than the work, load state once per worker, or try a free-threaded build.

  • The one big idea: Python is a fast language for arranging work and a slow one for doing it, so performance work is arranging more per interpreted step, after measuring which steps matter.

  • The two most-confused pairs: tottime vs cumtime (59: own work vs work including callees) · slow vs not scalable (58: per-request speed is algorithms and C; throughput is concurrency and scale-out).

  • Ten minutes before an interview: 58's two-lanes flowchart, 59's tracer-vs-sampler sequence diagram, 61's GIL-release sequence diagram, then this tree.

  • Cross-chapter: the eval loop (where the nanoseconds go) · the GIL (what native code releases) · diagnosing memory (the other axis profiling doesn't see).

notes.title: Why Python Is "Slow" — And Where It Isn't
notes.html:
📚 References

📘 Design and history FAQ · 📜 PEP 659: specializing adaptive interpreter · 📘 NumPy: broadcasting · 📖 GfG: Vectorization in Python

⚡ TL;DR

Python charges ~5–15 ns and an object header for every step it interprets; work handed to C costs ~1 ns per element and no header. So don't make the steps faster, have fewer of them: algorithm, then batch, then vectorize. Profile first.

🧭 Flow: bytecode instruction ─▶ eval loop dispatches it ─▶ operands are boxed PyObjects: type check, unbox ─▶ result is a new heap object ─▶ refcounts updated ─▶ repeat per element (~15 ns) ─▶ or one call into C walks contiguous memory (~1 ns per element)

🎯 Recall

Prompt Answer
Why is a Python loop slow? Per-step dispatch plus boxed objects: ~16 ns per iteration against ~0.5 ns in C.
What's the first thing to try? The algorithm: set membership beat list membership ~2,500×, no C involved.
What does vectorizing change? One interpreted call instead of N, and contiguous typed memory instead of pointers to objects.
Does the GIL make single-threaded code slow? No: it limits CPU-bound threads, a separate axis.
When is "Python is slow" irrelevant? When the service is I/O-bound: 40 ms of database, 2 ms of Python.
✏️ Draw by hand: two lanes Interpreted: dispatch ─▶ unbox ─▶ allocate ─▶ refcount, per element. Batched: one call ─▶ contiguous array ─▶ C/SIMD loop.

💡 The idea

Every operation in a Python loop goes through the interpreter and works on heap-allocated objects:

total = 0
for i in range(5_000_000):
    total += i          # advance iterator, load, int.__add__ allocates a NEW int, store
# CPython 3.12: 79 ms, ~16 ns per iteration.  Same loop in C (clang -O2): 2.5 ms.

Memory tells the same story: one million floats take 32.4 MB as a list (an 8 MB pointer array plus a million 24-byte float objects, see the object header) against 8.0 MB as a NumPy array. But the toll is charged only on operations Python performs. scores = matrix @ query is one interpreted step and millions of native multiply-adds. Python isn't uniformly slow; it's slow per interpreted step and roughly C-fast for work it delegates. The skill is knowing which side your hot code is on.

The trade: Python charges a fixed toll per interpreted step in exchange for being dynamic and quick to write, and the way out is arranging far fewer steps, not shaving each one.

⚙️ How it works

The two lanes the same computation can take:

Rule What actually happens
The per-operation toll On 3.12: a + b 6.3 ns, p.x 4.7 ns, d[k] 6.2 ns, f() 11.9 ns, o.m() 13.2 ns. Nothing is catastrophic, but ten operations per item over a million items is 50–130 ms before any useful work.
Specialization claws some back Since 3.11 a warm instruction is rewritten in place for the types it sees (an int-only add with a guard) (the eval loop). The loop is still interpreted.
Layout is half the win NumPy's array is one block of raw floats, so the CPU prefetches and vectorizes, and never touches a refcount. A C extension that still handles Python objects per element is nothing like as fast.
The GIL is a separate axis It blocks CPU-bound threads (the GIL), not a single loop; most C libraries release it while they work.

💻 Code

Retrieval top-k over 50,000 embeddings, once as an interpreted loop and once as a batched call:

import time, numpy as np
DIM, N = 384, 50_000
rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
mat = rng.standard_normal((N, DIM), dtype=np.float32)
mat /= np.linalg.norm(mat, axis=1, keepdims=True)
rows = [v.tolist() for v in mat]                 # what a JSON or DB layer hands you
query = mat[7].tolist()

def top_k_python(query, rows, k=5):              # ❌ DIM interpreted steps per document
    scored = []
    for i, row in enumerate(rows):
        dot = 0.0
        for a, b in zip(query, row):
            dot += a * b
        scored.append((dot, i))
    scored.sort(reverse=True)
    return scored[:k]

def top_k_numpy(query, matrix, k=5):             # ✅ one C call over the whole batch
    scores = matrix @ np.asarray(query, dtype=np.float32)
    idx = np.argpartition(-scores, k)[:k]         # O(n) select, not a full sort
    idx = idx[np.argsort(-scores[idx])]
    return [(float(scores[i]), int(i)) for i in idx]

On CPython 3.12 with NumPy 2.5.3 the loop took 429 ms and the batch 2.5 ms, about 170×, with identical results (top=[7, 38395, 32979, 11988, 19098]). 19.2 million interpreted multiply-adds became one call, and argpartition replaced sorting 50,000 scores to read five. The bridge is where cost hides: .tolist() and re-boxing can cost more than the arithmetic, so keep vectors as one array from load time.

⚠️ Break it: every listicle micro-optimization, against moving the loop.

import operator, numpy as np
def slow(q, rows):
    out = []
    for row in rows:
        d = 0.0
        for a, b in zip(q, row): d += a * b
        out.append(d)
    return out
def micro_optimized(q, rows):                       # local binding, comprehension, map
    _sum, _map, _mul = sum, map, operator.mul
    return [_sum(_map(_mul, q, row)) for row in rows]
def vectorized(q, mat):
    return mat @ np.asarray(q, dtype=np.float32)
# 20,000 rows × 384 dims, timed with perf_counter
# look for: the ratios between the three
# naive model predicts: the tricks close most of the gap

On 3.12: 112 ms, 76 ms, 0.5 ms. The tricks are real (1.5×) and irrelevant: vectorizing gave ~220×. Shaving interpreted operations buys tens of percent; removing them buys orders of magnitude (micro-optimization traps).

🗣️ Interview

30-second answer: Every Python operation goes through the interpreter, which fetches and dispatches bytecode and checks types at run time, and every value is a heap object with a header, so arithmetic allocates and iteration chases pointers. A summing loop costs ~16 ns per iteration against ~0.5 ns in C. So the fix is structural: better algorithms, batching, and hot loops pushed into C libraries. Often none of it matters, because the service is waiting on I/O.

Q · Mechanism — What does CPython do for total += i, and what did 3.11+ change? The eval loop fetches BINARY_OP, pops two PyObject* operands and calls the type's slot: check both types, unbox the C values, add, and allocate a new int, since ints are immutable; then refcounts change and the result is stored. A compiler emits one add. Since 3.11, PEP 659 watches the types flowing through each instruction and rewrites warm ones into specialized forms with cheap guards, plus cheaper frames and inlined calls. It narrows the toll; it doesn't remove the interpreter.

Q · Failure — A RAG endpoint's p99 is 900 ms and the team proposes a Go rewrite. What do you do? Measure first: py-spy in production plus timing around each dependency. Usually embedding, vector search, the LLM and the database dominate; if 90% is waiting, Go moves a 60 ms slice. Then check in order: an N+1 query or per-item API call (batch it), sequential work that could be concurrent, a sync call blocking the event loop, a missing cache for repeated embeddings, and only then a CPU-bound loop. If one component truly is CPU-bound and can't vectorize, go native for that component.

Q · Design — Chunk, embed and index 10M documents. Where does Python cost you? Classify stages: chunking is CPU-bound Python (batch it, use Rust-backed tokenizers, a process pool sized to cores); embedding is GPU or a remote API; index writes are I/O. Design for throughput: bounded queues, back-pressure, checkpoints, and sharding across machines. It breaks on memory first: 10M × 384 float32 is 15 GB, ~4× more as lists, so memory-map it; process pools multiply memory and pay pickling per item; remote APIs rate-limit. I'd watch documents per second per stage and the queue depths.

⚖️ Compare

Lever Typical win (measured here) Cost
Better algorithm or data structure ~2,500× (set vs list membership) thinking; sometimes memory
Vectorize or batch into C ~100–220× on numeric loops a dependency; array-shaped data
Concurrency for I/O up to the fan-out factor async complexity
Process pool for CPU ≈ cores, minus pickling memory × workers
Micro-optimizations ~1.5× readability
Rewrite in another language only the Python slice very high

🚫 Pitfalls

  • ❌ "Python is slow because of the GIL"
    ✅ The GIL limits CPU-bound threads; single-thread cost is dispatch and boxing.
  • 🪞 "Local binding and comprehension tricks are where the speed is"
    ✅ 1.5× in Break it; vectorizing gave ~220×.
  • ❌ "NumPy is fast because C is fast"
    ✅ Half of it is layout: contiguous typed data, no per-element objects or refcounts, SIMD-friendly.
  • 🔀 Not the same as scalability
    ↳ Difference: 2× faster per request is algorithms and C; 2× the concurrent requests is concurrency, pooling and scale-out.
  • ⚠️ Don't add NumPy for small n.
    ↳ Why: for a few hundred items, conversion overhead can exceed the loop.
  • ⚠️ Don't propose a rewrite before profiling.
    ↳ Rule: first name the percentage of wall time spent in Python frames.
  • 🔖 Version: specialization (PEP 659) 3.11+; the experimental JIT and free-threaded builds 3.13+ (interpreter speedups).
    ↳ Note: measured on CPython 3.12.13, Apple silicon, NumPy 2.5.3; ratios travel, absolute numbers don't.

🕸️ Connections

Path: eval loop ─▶ why Python is slow ─▶ profiling ─▶ the native boundary

  • Builds on the object header: why every value costs 24+ bytes and a refcount.
  • Builds on the eval loop: where the per-operation nanoseconds go.
  • Used by profiling: measure which lane the time is really in.
  • Contrasts with async I/O: the right lever when the time is spent waiting, not computing.
  • Same idea elsewhere: the JVM and V8 JIT-compile hot loops; Python delegates them to native libraries instead.

notes.title: Profiling the Right Way
notes.html:
📚 References

📘 The Python profilers · 📘 py-spy: sampling in production · 📘 line_profiler / kernprof · 📖 GfG: Profiling in Python

⚡ TL;DR

Wall vs CPU first, then cProfile sorted by tottime (own work) and cumtime (subsystem), then line_profiler on the winner. In production never trace: sample with py-spy. Measure the same workload before and after.

🧭 Flow: wall (perf_counter) vs CPU (process_time): the gap is waiting ─▶ cProfile the run ─▶ sort by tottime to find the function ─▶ line_profiler on that one function to find the line ─▶ fix ─▶ re-measure the same workload ─▶ in production: py-spy record --pid

🎯 Recall

Prompt Answer
tottime vs cumtime? tottime excludes callees (what to change); cumtime includes them (which subsystem costs).
Why not cProfile in production? Overhead scales with call count, ~3× on call-heavy code, and it needs a restart. Use py-spy.
How does a sampling profiler work? Another process reads the target's stacks ~100×/s: a few percent overhead, statistical results.
Wall vs CPU time? perf_counter vs process_time; the gap is I/O, locks and sleep.
What comes after cProfile names a function? line_profiler on that function: cProfile has no per-line view.
✏️ Draw by hand: tracer vs sampler Tracer: a hook inside the process on every call/return. Sampler: a separate process reading the stack ~100×/s.

💡 The idea

Intuition reads code, not time. In this ingestion loop the "obviously expensive" line is the SHA-256:

def ingest(docs):
    seen, kept = [], 0
    for i, doc in enumerate(docs):
        key = fingerprint(normalize(doc))   # sha256: "this must be the cost"
        if deduplicate(seen, key):          # `key in seen` on a list: "basically free"
            kept += 1
        if i % 500 == 0: time.sleep(0.00625)  # stands in for an I/O wait

Timing the whole run says 1.26 s and nothing more. cProfile attributes it on CPython 3.12:

   ncalls  tottime  percall  cumtime  percall filename:lineno(function)
    20000    0.905    0.000    0.906    0.000 ingest.py:6(deduplicate)
       40    0.294    0.007    0.294    0.007 {built-in method time.sleep}
    20000    0.017    0.000    0.017    0.000 {method 'findall' of 're.Pattern' objects}

The hash doesn't make the list; deduplicate is 72% of the run. And the same run printed wall 1.26s cpu 0.94s: the 0.32 s gap is sleep, waiting that no CPU optimization can recover.

The trade: profiling replaces a guess with a measurement, and in exchange every instrument distorts or omits something, so you pick the one that matches the question.

⚙️ How it works

Why the two kinds of profiler cost so differently:

Rule What actually happens
Deterministic (cProfile) A C hook on call, return and exception events: exact counts, and a tax on every call. It's wall time by default, which is why sleep showed 0.294 s.
Line (line_profiler) Instruments only registered functions, line by line. Heavy, so it's the second pass on a known hotspot.
Sampling (py-spy, austin) Attaches by PID with no code change or restart; dump shows every thread's stack in a hang. Short, rare functions may never be sampled. Needs root on macOS, SYS_PTRACE in containers.
Blind spots C extensions are one opaque row (findall); cProfile traces one thread; memory is a separate axis (tracemalloc).

💻 Code

The workflow: profile the run, rank by tottime, then go line by line on the winner.

import cProfile, pstats, time
from line_profiler import LineProfiler
import ingest as m

t0, c0 = time.perf_counter(), time.process_time()
cProfile.run("m.ingest(m.DOCS)", "prof.out")             # stats file, not text
wall, cpu = time.perf_counter() - t0, time.process_time() - c0
print(f"wall {wall:.2f}s  cpu {cpu:.2f}s  waiting {wall - cpu:.2f}s")
st = pstats.Stats("prof.out").strip_dirs()
st.sort_stats("tottime").print_stats(6)        # own work → what to change
# st.sort_stats("cumtime").print_stats(6)      # subsystem cost
# st.print_callers("deduplicate")              # who calls the hotspot?

lp = LineProfiler()
lp.add_function(m.deduplicate)                 # only what pass 1 implicated
lp.runcall(m.ingest, m.DOCS[:5000])            # smaller slice: line profiling is heavy
lp.print_stats(output_unit=1e-3)

py-spy top --pid 4242                          # live view of Python frames
py-spy record --pid 4242 -d 30 -o flame.svg    # 30 s flamegraph, no restart
py-spy dump --pid 4242                         # every thread's stack now (a hang)

line_profiler 5.0.2 put 97.7% of deduplicate on if key in seen:, a linear scan of a growing list, O(n²) over the corpus. The fix is a set, not a faster hash. cProfile narrowed 15 functions to one, line_profiler one function to one line, and the line named the bug.

⚠️ Break it: the profiler changes the ranking it reports.

import cProfile, pstats, time
def tiny(x): return x * 2
def many_small_calls(n):                 # 2M cheap function calls
    t = 0
    for i in range(n): t += tiny(i)
    return t
def one_big_loop(n):                     # the same arithmetic, inline
    t = 0
    for i in range(n): t += i * 2
    return t
# time each with perf_counter, then both under one cProfile.Profile()
# look for: the ratio between the two, real vs profiled
# naive model predicts: the profiler preserves the ranking

On 3.12 the real times were 69.9 ms vs 47.3 ms, 1.5×. Under cProfile, cumtime was 0.187 vs 0.048, 3.9×: two million call events were charged to the first function. A cProfile ranking is work + call overhead, so confirm surprises against wall time or a sampler, which has no such bias.

🗣️ Interview

30-second answer: First separate waiting from computing, wall time against process_time, because if most of it is I/O, CPU profiling is the wrong tool. Locally, cProfile with pstats: tottime finds the function doing the work itself, cumtime the subsystem it sits under. Then line_profiler on that function finds the line. In production I attach py-spy to the running process: it samples from outside, costs a few percent, and needs no restart.

Q · Mechanism — Deterministic vs sampling: how does each work, and what does each get wrong? cProfile registers a C callback on CPython's call and return events, so counts are exact but the cost is proportional to the number of calls, not the work: 2 million tiny calls inflated a 1.5× ratio to 3.9× (see Break it). That biases rankings toward call-heavy code and rules it out on latency-sensitive services. py-spy runs as a separate process reading the target's memory ~100 times a second: a few percent, no instrumentation. What it gets wrong is the tail: short or rare functions may never be sampled.

Q · Failure — An async FastAPI service has good average latency but a bad p99, and a local cProfile of the handler shows nothing. What's going on? The time isn't in the handler's CPU; it's a blocking call on the event loop (a sync driver, requests, a big JSON parse) that freezes every other request on that worker, which one handler run locally can't reproduce. Turn on asyncio debug mode, which logs callbacks over 100 ms and often names the offender; py-spy record a loaded worker and look for synchronous frames under the loop; add per-dependency timing and read histogram percentiles, not averages.

Q · Design — Continuous performance visibility for a fleet, catching regressions before customers do. Three layers: RED metrics with latency histograms, always on; OpenTelemetry tracing around each dependency, head-sampled with tail sampling for slow or failed traces; and continuous sampling profiles labelled by release, diffed across deploys. Trace IDs in every log line tie them together. Budget overhead explicitly (metrics <1%, tracing <2%, profiling a few percent). It breaks where samplers miss rare requests, C frames are opaque, and async time is hard to attribute. I'd watch p99 per endpoint per release first.

⚖️ Compare

Tool Kind Overhead Granularity Production?
perf_counter / process_time manual ~0 whatever you wrap ✅
cProfile + pstats deterministic ~3× on call-heavy code per function ❌
line_profiler deterministic heavy, targeted per line ❌
py-spy / austin sampling a few % per stack frame ✅ attach by PID
perf + -X perf (3.12+) OS sampling low native + Python frames ✅ Linux

🚫 Pitfalls

  • ❌ "The profiler's ranking is the truth"
    ✅ cProfile taxes call frequency: 3.9× reported vs 1.5× real (see Break it).
  • 🪞 "Sort by cumtime: the biggest number is the hotspot"
    ✅ cumtime on main is always ~100%.
    ↳ Rule: tottime finds the code to change; cumtime finds the subsystem to blame.
  • ❌ "A local profile represents production"
    ✅ Production has concurrency, cold caches, real data sizes and network latency: sample the live process.
  • 🔀 Not the same as monitoring
    ↳ Difference: a profiler says which code spent the time in this run; monitoring says is it slow now, and since when.
  • ⚠️ Don't profile CPU when wall ≫ CPU.
    ↳ Why: the time is waiting; find what blocks instead.
  • ⚠️ Don't leave @profile decorators in committed code.
    ↳ Why: a several-fold slowdown, and only kernprof defines the name.
  • 🔖 Version: -X perf and sys.monitoring (PEP 669, cheaper event hooks for new tools) are 3.12+.
    ↳ Note: measured on CPython 3.12.13 with line_profiler 5.0.2; ratios travel, absolute numbers don't.

🕸️ Connections

Path: why Python is slow ─▶ profiling ─▶ micro-optimization traps

  • Builds on why Python is slow: what you're looking for, and which levers are worth pulling.
  • Used by micro-optimization traps: timeit for the before/after once the hotspot is known.
  • Contrasts with diagnosing memory: the same question on the memory axis, with tracemalloc.
  • Used by observability: continuous profiling and tracing are this, always on.
  • Same idea elsewhere: Java's async-profiler and Go's pprof are samplers for the same reason: tracing every call distorts a live service.

notes.title: Micro-Optimization Traps
notes.html:
📚 References

📘 timeit: autorange and GC behaviour · 📘 Programming FAQ: concatenating many strings · 📖 GfG: timeit in Python

⚡ TL;DR

timeit measures one statement with the GC off, constants folded and only the best run: precise, and often about nothing. Profile first; fix the algorithm (join, set, comprehension); treat listicle tricks as noise until measured at real n.

🧭 Flow: timeit.repeat(stmt, setup) ─▶ compile stmt: constant expressions folded ─▶ gc.disable() ─▶ run N times, warm caches, no surrounding program ─▶ report min of repeats ─▶ transferable only if n, types and GC pressure match production

🎯 Recall

Prompt Answer
What does timeit hide? It disables GC, folds constants, reports min, and runs with no surrounding program state.
Is s += piece in a loop O(n²)? Only where the in-place optimization can't apply: self.s += measured 25× slower than join.
Do the classic tricks still pay? Hoisting append is now slower; local binding gives 6–10%: rarely worth the readability.

💡 The idea

A timeit one-liner will confirm differences that don't exist in your program. On CPython 3.12, python -m timeit "2**20" reported 2.9 ns: the compiler folded the constant before timing started. The same arithmetic through variables took 28 ns. Re-measured on 3.12, most listicle advice has aged (the Compare table): hoisting out.append is now slower, map with a lambda is 2× slower than a comprehension, and the one claim that's still dramatic, string +=, is true only on an attribute.

The trade: micro-benchmarks are cheap and precise, and precision about the wrong thing is how a team spends a week making code uglier for a percent that profiling never asked for.

⚙️ How it works

Rule What actually happens
GC off on purpose timeit disables the collector so repeats are comparable, which hides allocation cost. Building 50,000 dicts: 2.1 vs 2.2 ms on 3.12, but 2.4 vs 3.2 ms on 3.14, a third more (the collector). Pass setup="gc.enable()" for code that allocates.
min is not the average The best run filters scheduling noise: right for comparing two versions, wrong as a prediction of production latency, where the tail matters.
Why old tricks stopped paying Since 3.11 the specializing interpreter caches global and attribute lookups inline; hoisting list.append into a local defeats the specialized method-call path, which is why it's slower.
The real one is algorithmic CPython resizes s += piece in place when s is a local holding the only reference. On an attribute (self.s +=) it can't, so each step copies: 25× join. That's a bug shape, not a micro-optimization.

💻 Code

A benchmark harness that doesn't lie to you:

import timeit, statistics

def bench(stmt: str, setup: str = "pass", *, n: int, gc_on: bool = True, repeat: int = 7):
    """Time `stmt` the way the program will actually run it."""
    setup = ("import gc; gc.enable()\n" if gc_on else "") + setup   # timeit turns GC off
    per_call = [t / n for t in timeit.repeat(stmt, setup, number=n, repeat=repeat)]
    return min(per_call), statistics.median(per_call)               # best AND typical

REAL_N = 2_000                                   # the size production sees, not 10
SETUP = f"items = [str(i) for i in range({REAL_N})]"
for label, stmt in [
    ("join",       '"".join(items)'),
    ("s += local", 's = ""\nfor i in items: s += i'),
    ("list+join",  'buf = []\nfor i in items: buf.append(i)\n"".join(buf)'),
]:
    best, med = bench(stmt, SETUP, n=2_000)
    print(f"{label:12s} best {best*1e6:7.1f} us   median {med*1e6:7.1f} us")
# Traps avoided: GC left on; data built in setup, not timed; real n, because O(n²)
# hides at n=10; median as well as min; no literal constants (2**20 folds to 2.9 ns).

The rule this encodes matters more than any single result: a micro-benchmark is evidence only when the profiler has already named the code as hot, and when n and types match production.

🗣️ Interview

30-second answer: Almost none, until a profiler has named the code. What keeps paying is algorithmic: "".join over repeated concatenation, a set over a linear scan, comprehensions over append loops (~20%), and not redoing work inside a loop. The listicle tricks have mostly evaporated: hoisting append measured slower on 3.12 and 3.14, and binding globals to locals gives single-digit percent. Profile, fix the algorithm, then measure before and after on production-sized data.

Q · Mechanism — timeit says A is 30% faster than B, but the service shows no difference. Why? timeit turns the GC off, so the version that allocates more looks better; on 3.14 that hid a third of the cost of building dicts. It reports the minimum, filtering out the tail. It runs in a tight loop with warm caches and fully specialized bytecode, unlike the cold, interleaved path in a request. Then proportion: if the function is 2% of the request, a 30% win is 0.6%, invisible next to network jitter.

⚖️ Compare

Trick Measured on 3.12 [3.14] Worth it?
"".join(parts) vs s += (2,000 pieces) 5.2 vs 43 µs local, 133 µs on self.s ✅ always
Comprehension vs for + append 11.6 vs 14.1 µs [12.2 vs 14.2] ✅ readability + ~20%
map(lambda …) vs comprehension 25.5 vs 11.6 µs [22.3 vs 12.2] ❌ slower
Hoisting out.append 15.5 vs 14.1 µs [15.7 vs 14.2] ❌ slower now
Binding a global to a local 1.48 vs 1.58 µs [1.66 vs 1.85] ⚪ 6–10%, rarely worth it

🚫 Pitfalls

  • ❌ "timeit gives the real cost of this code"
    ✅ GC off, constants folded, min of repeats, no surrounding program.
    ↳ Fix: gc.enable() in setup, real n, report the median too.
  • 🪞 "Hoisting append and local binding are free wins"
    ✅ Hoisting is ~10% slower; local binding is a few percent. Specialization already does the work.
  • ❌ "String += in a loop is always quadratic"
    ✅ CPython optimizes the local-variable case in place; it's quadratic on attributes, list elements and shared references, exactly where people write it.
  • ⚠️ Don't micro-optimize before profiling.
    ↳ Why: a 30% win on 2% of the time is 0.6%.
  • ⚠️ Don't trust a benchmark at toy n.
    ↳ Why: algorithmic differences only appear at real size.
  • 🔖 Version: PEP 659 specialization (3.11+) turned hoisting and local binding from wins into losses or small change; 3.14's GC changed allocation costs.
    ↳ Note: measured on CPython 3.12.13 and 3.14.6 (Apple silicon), indicative only.

🕸️ Connections

Path: profiling ─▶ micro-optimization traps ─▶ the native boundary

  • Builds on profiling: the step that must come first.
  • Contrasts with why Python is slow: the ~1.5× lane next to the 100× lane of vectorizing.
  • Breaks when combined with interpreter speedups: specialization is what retired these tricks.
  • Same idea elsewhere: JMH in Java exists because naive JVM micro-benchmarks fold, inline and warm up their way to wrong answers too.

notes.title: The C-Extension & Native Acceleration Boundary
notes.html:
📚 References

📘 ctypes · 📘 C API: thread state and the GIL · 📘 Cython: building code · 📖 GfG: Using C code in Python

⚡ TL;DR

Native code removes the per-operation toll and can release the GIL, but charges per crossing: ~21 ns compiled, ~113 ns through ctypes. So batch the interface (NumPy's break-even was ~200 items per call), and check for an existing library first.

🧭 Flow: Python calls the extension ─▶ convert arguments (or take a buffer pointer, no copy) while holding the GIL ─▶ Py_BEGIN_ALLOW_THREADS ─▶ C loop over raw memory while other threads run ─▶ Py_END_ALLOW_THREADS ─▶ build one result object

🎯 Recall

Prompt Answer
What decides whether going native pays? Work per crossing: ~21 ns (C-API) to ~113 ns (ctypes) per call; NumPy beat sum(list) only from ~200 items.
Why do C extensions help with threads? They release the GIL: four threads of np.sort did 4× the work in 1.05× the time.
ctypes vs Cython vs PyO3? ctypes: no build, slowest, unsafe signatures. Cython: annotated Python, compiled. PyO3: Rust, memory-safe, where new work goes.

💡 The idea

"Rewrite the hot part in C" sounds like a switch, but the win depends on how often you cross the boundary. On CPython 3.12 with NumPy 2.5.3:

n sum(list) arr.sum() winner
10 51 ns 226 ns Python
100 158 ns 238 ns Python
200 270 ns 243 ns native, just
10,000 12.6 µs 1.35 µs native, 9×

NumPy's fixed cost per call is ~230 ns, so below ~200 elements the boundary costs more than the work. The second, quieter reason to go native is the GIL: a pure-Python loop in four threads took 3.94× as long as one, while four threads of np.sort took 1.05×, near-linear scaling in CPython threads.

The trade: native code removes the per-operation toll and the GIL from the hot loop, in exchange for a fixed per-call cost, a build toolchain, and bugs that segfault instead of raising.

⚙️ How it works

One crossing, and the promise that releasing the GIL requires:

Rule What actually happens
What a crossing costs Converting arguments and the result, plus refcounts. ctypes interprets the signature at run time (113 ns); a compiled extension does it in generated code (math.sqrt, 21 ns). Batch APIs convert once via the buffer protocol, a pointer to existing memory.
Releasing the GIL is a promise Between the two macros the extension may not touch any Python object (no refcounts, allocation or callbacks), because other threads are running the interpreter. Break it and refcounts corrupt.

💻 Code

The decision in code: FFI per call, bulk vs per item, and the thread test that shows the GIL being released.

import ctypes, ctypes.util, threading, time
import numpy as np

libm = ctypes.CDLL(ctypes.util.find_library("m"))
libm.sqrt.restype  = ctypes.c_double         # WITHOUT these, ctypes assumes int:
libm.sqrt.argtypes = [ctypes.c_double]       # sqrt(2.0) came back as 1801344768

def scores_per_item(vectors, q):             # ❌ ~230 ns of boundary per row
    return [float(np.dot(v, q)) for v in vectors]
def scores_batched(matrix, q):               # ✅ one crossing for the whole batch
    return matrix @ q

arrays = [np.random.rand(2_000_000) for _ in range(4)]
def run(n_threads, target):
    ts = [threading.Thread(target=target, args=(i,)) for i in range(n_threads)]
    t0 = time.perf_counter(); [t.start() for t in ts]; [t.join() for t in ts]
    return time.perf_counter() - t0
def native(i): np.sort(arrays[i])            # releases the GIL while sorting
def pure(_):
    t = 0
    for k in range(2_000_000): t += k        # holds the GIL throughout
for name, fn in (("np.sort", native), ("python loop", pure)):
    print(name, f"4x work in {run(4, fn) / run(1, fn):.2f}x time")

With OMP_NUM_THREADS=1 so BLAS added no threads of its own: np.sort 1.05×, the Python loop 3.94×, the GIL visible in one line. The restype line is the dangerous lesson: an unset signature returned 1801344768 for √2 with no error.

🗣️ Interview

30-second answer: Only after profiling names a specific CPU-bound function, and only if no library (numpy, polars, orjson, tokenizers) already does it. Then the deciding factor is work per crossing: ~20 ns per call compiled, over 100 ns via ctypes, so batch APIs win and per-item ones lose. The second payoff is threads: a native extension can release the GIL. Against that: a toolchain, wheels per platform, and segfaults. Cython for Python-shaped code, PyO3 for new substantial work.

Q · Mechanism — What happens when Python calls into a C extension, and what does releasing the GIL require? The extension receives PyObject* arguments and converts them: unboxing numbers, or requesting a buffer for arrays, which yields a raw pointer without copying. It computes, builds a result object and manages refcounts throughout; that's the fixed per-call cost. Releasing the GIL is bracketed: between Py_BEGIN_ALLOW_THREADS and Py_END_ALLOW_THREADS it may not touch any Python object, because other threads are executing bytecode. So the shape is always convert, release, compute on raw memory, re-acquire, build.

⚖️ Compare

Route Build step Per-call cost Safety Use when
Existing C/Rust library none the library's ✅ almost always: check first
ctypes / cffi none / optional ~113 ns (ctypes) ❌ wrong signature = garbage or segfault calling an existing .so, few calls
Cython compiler + wheels ~C-API ✅ mostly hot Python-shaped loops
C-API extension compiler + wheels ~21 ns ❌ manual refcounts maximum control
PyO3 / Rust Rust + maturin ~C-API ✅ memory-safe substantial new native work

🚫 Pitfalls

  • ❌ "The GIL makes threads useless in Python"
    ✅ It makes pure-Python threads useless; native code that releases it scaled 4× work in 1.05× time.
  • 🪞 "ctypes is a cheap way to speed up a hot loop"
    ✅ It's the most expensive crossing: for reusing an existing library, not for speed.
  • ⚠️ Don't omit restype and argtypes.
    ↳ Why: ctypes assumes int and returns garbage, silently.
  • ⚠️ Don't underestimate distribution.
    ↳ Why: wheels per platform and Python version, or users compile from source; the stable ABI (abi3) avoids per-version rebuilds.
  • 🔖 Version: free-threaded builds (3.13+, supported in 3.14) need extensions to declare and prove thread-safety (interpreter speedups).
    ↳ Note: measured on CPython 3.12.13, NumPy 2.5.3, Apple silicon.

🕸️ Connections

Path: why Python is slow ─▶ the native boundary ─▶ interpreter speedups

  • Builds on why Python is slow: the per-operation toll this removes.
  • Builds on the GIL: what native code releases, and why threads then scale.
  • Contrasts with multiprocessing: CPU parallelism without native code, paid in pickling and memory.
  • Same mechanism as threading for I/O: blocking I/O calls release the GIL the same way.
  • Same idea elsewhere: Java's JNI and Node's N-API carry the same per-crossing cost, so they also favour batch interfaces.

notes.title: Interpreter-Level Speedups
notes.html:
📚 References

📜 PEP 659: specializing adaptive interpreter · 📜 PEP 744: JIT compilation · 📜 PEP 703: free threading · 📘 Free-threading HOWTO

⚡ TL;DR

3.11+ rewrites warm bytecode in place for the types it sees (BINARY_OP → BINARY_OP_ADD_INT); 3.13+ adds an opt-in JIT and a no-GIL build. Upgrading is the cheapest ~1.2–1.4× you'll get, and it's why the old micro-optimization tricks stopped paying.

🎯 Recall

Prompt Answer
What is a specializing adaptive interpreter? 3.11+ (PEP 659): warm instructions are rewritten in place as type-specialized ones with guards.
What does dis(..., adaptive=True) show? The specialized opcodes actually in use, e.g. BINARY_OP_ADD_INT.
JIT and free threading: which versions? Opt-in experimental JIT 3.13+ (PEP 744); free-threaded builds 3.13+, supported in 3.14 (PEP 703).

💡 The idea

Before 3.11 the eval loop ran the same generic bytecode every time; nothing learned was reused. The Faster CPython work made it adaptive: once an instruction is warm and its types are stable, it's rewritten as a specialized form with a cheap guard. 3.11 was advertised at ~1.25× over 3.10. Free-threaded builds trade some single-thread speed for real thread parallelism. Upgrading beats micro-optimizing and loses to vectorizing.

💻 Code

import dis, sys
def add(a, b): return a + b
for _ in range(100): add(1, 2)                         # warm up with ints
print([i.opname for i in dis.get_instructions(add, adaptive=True)])
print(sys.version_info >= (3, 13) and sys._is_gil_enabled())
# 3.12  → ['RESUME', 'LOAD_FAST__LOAD_FAST', 'LOAD_FAST', 'BINARY_OP_ADD_INT', 'RETURN_VALUE']
# 3.14  → ['RESUME_CHECK', 'LOAD_FAST_BORROW_LOAD_FAST_BORROW', 'BINARY_OP_ADD_INT', 'RETURN_VALUE'], True
# 3.14t → same opcodes, then False: the GIL is off
